{{smaller block|<poem>Of any mind what other mind may judge
Save God, who only knows the thing He made,
The ''veritable'' service He exacts?</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 218.}}}}
'''2.''' Truthful; veracious.
{{smaller block|In verities he was very ''veritable''. {{right|''Golden Book'', xiv.}}}}

'''veritably''' (ver′i-ta̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a veritable or true manner; verily; truly; genuinely.

'''3.''' In ''gilding'', a liquid composed of arnotto, gamboge, vermilion, dragon’s-blood, salt of tartar, and saffron, boiled in water and applied to a surface that is to be gilded, to give luster to the gold. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''4.''' A crimson-red garnet inclining slightly to orange: a jewelers’ name.

¶
'''vermeiled†''', ''a.'' [Also ''vermiled''; < ''vermeil'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Gilded.
{{smaller block|The presses painted and ''vermiled'' with gold.
{{right|''Ph. de Commines'', D d 3.}}
It is all of square marble, and all the front ''vermiled'' with golde.
{{right|''Ibid.'' (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''vermelet†''', ''n.'' [< OF. ''vermeillet'', somewhat red, dim. of ''vermeil'', red: see ''vermeil.''] Vermilion.
{{smaller block|<poem>O bright Regina, who made the so faire?
Who made thy colour ''vermelet'' and white?</poem>
{{right|''Court of Love'', l. 142.}}}}

'''vermeologist''' (vėr-mẹ̄-ol′ọ̄-jist), ''n.'' [< ''vermeolog-y'' + ''-ist.''] One who is versed in vermeology; a helminthologist.

'''vermeology''' (vėr-mẹ̄-ol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [Irreg. < L. ''vermis'', a worm (> NL. ''Vermes'', the worms), + Gr. ''-λογία'', < λέγειν, speak: see ''-ology.''] The knowledge or description of worms; that branch of zoölogy which treats of the ''Vermes''; helminthology.

'''Vermes''' (vėr′mēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of L. ''vermis'', a worm, = E. ''worm.''] '''1.''' Worms: formerly including animals resembling the common earthworm, but having no exact classificatory sense, and hence no standing in zoölogy.—'''2†.''' The sixth and last division of animals in the Lin-

'''3.''' One of the eight primary divisions of the animal kingdom; a subkingdom or phylum, one of the leading types of animal life, comprising all those animals which have a body-cavity (''Metazoa''), no backbone (''Invertebrata''), normally an intestinal canal (which ''Cœlentera'' have not), not a radiate structure (which ''Echinodermata'' have), legs if any not jointed (they are always jointed in ''Arthropoda''), and body vermiform if there are no legs. {{smaller|In this acceptation ''Vermes'' form a most comprehensive group, of great diversity of form, but agreeing in certain fundamental structural characters, being generally soft vermiform animals, oftenest segmented and bilaterally symmetrical, without limbs or with unjointed limbs. ''Vermes'' thus defined are approximately equivalent—(''a'') in Lamarck’s system (1801–1812), to a class of animals divided into the four orders ''Molles'', ''Rigiduli'', ''Hispiduli'', and ''Epizoariæ'' (the last including lernæan crustaceans); (''b'') in the Cuvierian classification (1817), to the whole of Cuvier’s first class of ''Articulata'' (the annelids of Lamarck, or red-blooded worms with unjointed legs) plus his second and third classes of ''Radiata'' (''Apoda'' and ''Entozoa''), plus some of his fourth class of ''Radiata'' (some ''Polypi''), plus his first order (''Rotifera'') of his fifth class of ''Radiata''; (''c'') in Huxley’s classification (1869), to the classes ''Polyzoa'', ''Scolecida'', ''Annelida'', ''Chætognatha'', and therefore to his two subkingdoms, ''Annuloida'' and ''Annulosa'', without the ''Echinodermata'' of the former, and}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|verify|6729|Vermetidæ}}</noinclude>that the statements in it are true. (''b'') To support by proof or by argument. ='''Syn. 1, 3''', and '''4'''. {{smaller|To authenticate, substantiate, corroborate, attest.}}

'''veriloquent†''' (vẹ̄-ril′ọ̄-kwent), ''a.'' [< L. ''verus'', true, + ''loquen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''loqui'', speak.] Speaking truth; truthful; truth-telling; veracious.

'''verily''' (ver′i-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''verili, verrili, veraily, verraly, verreiliche''; < ''very'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' In truth; in very truth or deed; beyond doubt or question; certainly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thi loue is to us euerelastynge
Fro that tyme that we may it ''verrili'' fele.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}
But the centurien . . . seide, ''Verili'', this man was Goddis sone.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Mark xv. 39.}}
''Verily'' some such matter it was as want of a fat Dioces that kept our Britain Bishops so poore in the primitive times.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
'''2.''' Really; truly; in sincere earnestness; with conviction and confidence: as, he ''verily'' believes the woman’s story.
{{smaller block|It was ''verily'' thought that, had it not been for four great disfavourers of that voyage, the enterprize had succeeded.
{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

'''veriment†''', ''adv.'' [ME., also ''verrayment, verament'', < OF. ''veraiement'', F. ''vraiment'', truly, < ''verai, vrai'', true: see ''very''.] Truly; verily.
{{smaller block|<poem>I wol telle ''verrayment''
Of mirthe and of solas.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Sir Thopas, l. 2.}}}}

'''veriment†''', ''n.'' [Also ''verament''; an erroneous use, as a noun, of ''veriment, adv.''] Truth; ver-

ity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell unto you
What is ''veriment'' and true.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Friar Bacon, p. 164. (''Davies.'')}}
In ''verament'' and sincerity, I never crouded through this confluent Herring-faire.
{{right|''Nashe'', Lenten Stuffe (Harl. Misc., VI. 162). (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''verisimilar''' (ver-i-sim′i-lär), ''a.'' [After ''similar'' (cf. Sp. ''verisimil'' = Pg. ''verisimil'' = It. ''verisimile''), < L. ''verisimilis'', prop. ''veri similis'', having the appearance of truth: ''veri'', gen. of ''verum'', truth (neut. of ''verus'', true); ''similis'', like: see ''very'' and ''similar''.] Having the appearance of truth; probable; likely.
{{smaller block|Various anecdotes of him [Dante] are related by Boccaccio, Sacchetti, and others, . . . none of them ''verisimilar.''
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 19.}}}}

'''verisimilarly''' (ver-i-sim′i-lä̤r-li), ''adv.'' In a verisimilar manner; probably.
{{smaller block|Wordsworth [was] talked of . . . [and] represented ''verisimilarly'' enough as a man full of English prejudices.
{{right|''Carlyle'', in Froude (First Forty Years), II. xiv.}}}}

'''verisimilitude''' (ver″i-si-mil′i-tūd), ''n.'' [= Sp. ''verisimilitud'' = Pg. ''verisimilitude'' = It. ''verisimilitudine'', < L. ''verisimilitudo'', prop. ''veri similitudo'', likeness to truth: ''veri'', gen. of ''verum'', truth; {{smaller block|''similitudo'', likeness: see ''similitude'', and cf. ''verisimilar''.]}}

Correction — the first lines are main text, not smaller:

''similitudo'', likeness: see ''similitude'', and cf. ''verisimilar''.] '''1.''' The quality or state of being verisimilar; the appearance of truth; probability; likelihood: as, the ''verisimilitude'' of a story.
{{smaller block|The story is as authentic as many histories, and the reader need only give such an amount of credence to it as he may judge that its ''verisimilitude'' warrants.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, iii.}}
These devices were adopted to heighten the ''verisimilitude'' of the scene. {{right|''Lathrop'', Spanish Vistas, p. 119.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is verisimilar; that which has the appearance of a verity or fact.
{{smaller block|Shadows of fact,—''verisimilitudes'', not verities.
{{right|''Lamb'', Old Benchers.}}}}

'''verisimility†''' (ver″i-si-mil′ị-ti), ''n.'' [< L. *''veri similita(t-)s'', equiv. to ''veri similitudo'', likeness to truth: see ''verisimilitude''.] Verisimilitude.
{{smaller block|The spirit of man cannot be satisfied but with truth or at least ''verisimility''. {{right|''Dryden'', Essay on Dram. Poesy.}}}}

'''verisimilous''' (ver-i-sim′i-lus), ''a.'' [< L. ''verisimilis'': see ''verisimilar''.] Probable; verisimilar.
{{smaller block|A fresh and more appalling, because more self-assertive and ''verisimilous'', invasion of the commonplace.
{{right|''Geo. MacDonald'', Thomas Wingfold, Curate, xli.}}}}

'''veritable''' (ver′i-ta-bl), ''a.'' [< OF. ''veritable'', F. ''véritable'' = It. ''veritevole'', true, < L. ''verita(t-)s'', truth: see ''verity''.] '''1.''' Agreeable to truth or fact; true; real; actual; genuine.
{{smaller block|Notwithstanding that their writings [those of the seventy-two Biblical interpreters] be ''veritable'', also it is in some matter obscure, and in other some diminished.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 381.}}
The inward work and worth <poem>Of any mind what other mind may judge
Save God, who only knows the thing He made,
The ''veritable'' service He exacts?</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 218.}}}}
'''2.''' Truthful; veracious.
{{smaller block|In verities he was very ''veritable''. {{right|''Golden Book'', xiv.}}}}

'''veritably''' (ver′i-ta̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a veritable or true manner; verily; truly; genuinely.

{{smaller block|When two augurs cannot meet each other with grave faces, their craft is ''veritably'' in danger.
{{right|''H. N. Oxenham'', Short Studies, p. 379.}}}}

'''veritas''' (ver′i-tas), ''n.'' [F. ''véritas'' (also ''bureau véritas''), < L. ''veritas'', truth: see ''verity''.] A name given to a register of shipping in France on the principle of Lloyd’s. The name has also been used for the same purpose in Norway and in Austria.

'''verity''' (ver′i̤-ti), ''n.''; pl. ''verities'' (-tiz). [Early mod. E. also ''veritie'', ''verytee''; < ME. ''verite'', < OF. ''verite'', F. ''vérité'' = Sp. ''verdad'' = Pg. ''verdade'' = It. ''verità'', < L. ''verita(t-)s'', truth, truthfulness, < ''verus'', true: see ''very''.] '''1.''' The quality of being true or real; true or real nature or principle; reality; truth; fact.
{{smaller block|Ffeire frende, now telle me what ye be, and of youre felowes telle me the ''verite'', ffor longe me thinketh it to wite.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 372.}}
<poem>So he gan do in trouth and ''uerite'',
As for to see hym gret pite it was,
His mornyng, his wailyng, his loking bas.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 665.}}
The Prelates thought the plaine and homespun ''verity'' of Christs Gospel unfit any longer to hold their Lordships acquaintance.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is true; a true assertion or tenet; a truth; a reality; a fact.
{{smaller block|<poem>Mark what I say, which you shall find
By every syllable a faithful ''verity''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 3. 131.}}
That which seems faintly possible, it is so refined, is often faint and dim because it is deeply seated in the mind among the eternal ''verities''.
{{right|''Emerson'', Nature, viii.}}}}
'''3†.''' Honesty; faith; trustworthiness. {{smaller block|Justice, ''verity'', temperance. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And fair Marg’ret, and rare Marg’ret,
And Marg’ret o’ ''veritie.''</poem>
{{right|''Clerk Saunders'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 52).}}}}

'''Of a verity''', in very truth or deed; certainly.
{{smaller block|''Of a verity'' his position denoted no excess of ease or enjoyment. {{right|''Lever'', Davenport Dunn, ii.}}}}

'''verjuice''' (vėr′jös), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''verjuyce'', ''verdjuice''; < ME. *''verjus'', ''verjous'', ''vergeous'', < OF. ''verjus'', verjuice, juice of green fruits, < ''verd'', green, + ''jus'', juice: see ''verd'' and ''juice''.] '''1.''' An acid liquor expressed from crab-apples, unripe grapes, etc., used for culinary and other purposes.
{{smaller block|<poem>ȝit Moyses this resoun rad,
“Ete ȝoure lambe with soure ''vergeous.''”</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 203.}}}}
{{smaller block|Having a crabbed face of her own, she’ll eat the less ''verjuice'' with her mutton. {{right|''Middleton'', Women Beware Women, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many leave roses and gather thistles, loathe honey and love ''verjuice.'' {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 550.}}}}
{{smaller block|I pray . . . get a good ship and forty hogsheads of meal, . . . a hogshead of wine vinegar, and another of ''verjuice'', both in good casks and iron-bound. {{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 454.}}}}
'''2.''' Sourness or acidity of temper, manner, or expression; tartness.

'''verjuice''' (vėr′jös), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''verjuiced'', ppr. ''verjuicing''. [< ''verjuice'', ''n.''] To make sour or acid.
{{smaller block|His sermons with satire are plenteously ''verjuiced.'' {{right|''Lowell'', Fable for Critics.}}}}

'''Vermale’s operation.''' See ''operation.''

'''vermayle†, vermeile†,''' ''n.'' Obsolete forms of ''vermeil.''
{{smaller block|<poem>For such another, as I gesse,
Aforne ne was, ne more ''vermayle.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose,'' l. 3645.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Early editions have the spelling ''vermeile.'' The French has ''vermeille.'']}}

'''vermeil''' (vėr′mil), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vermil, vermell'' (the mod. spelling being a reversion to the F. spelling); < ME. ''vermeile, vermayle,'' < OF. ''vermeil'' (= It. ''vermiglio''), bright red, vermilion, < L. ''vermiculus,'' a little worm, LL. (in Vulgate) used for the kermes-insect, from which the color crimson or carmine was obtained, dim. of L. ''vermis,'' a worm, = E. ''worm:'' see ''vermicle, vermicule,'' and ''worm,'' and cf. ''crimson'' and ''carmine,'' which are ult. connected with ''worm.'' Hence ''vermilion.''] '''1.''' A bright red; vermilion; the color of vermilion. Also used adjectively, and frequently as the first element of a compound. [Now only poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>How oft that day did sad Brunchildis see
The greene shield dyde in dolorous ''vermell?''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., II. x. 24.}}
A ''vermeil''-tinctured lip. {{right|''Milton,'' Comus, l. 752.}}
<poem>Daisies, ''vermeil''-rimm’d and white.</poem>
{{right|''Keats,'' Endymion, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Silver gilt.
{{smaller block|The iconostase or screen is a high wall of burnished ''vermeil,'' with five superposed rows of figures framed in richly ornamented cases of embossed metal.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.,'' LXXIX. 334.}}}} '''3.''' In ''gilding'', a liquid composed of arnotto, gamboge, vermilion, dragon’s-blood, salt of tartar, and saffron, boiled in water and applied to a surface that is to be gilded, to give luster to the gold. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''4.''' A crimson-red garnet inclining slightly to orange: a jewelers’ name.

'''vermeiled†''', ''a.'' [Also ''vermiled''; < ''vermeil'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Gilded.
{{smaller block|The presses painted and ''vermiled'' with gold.
{{right|''Ph. de Commines'', D d 3.}}
It is all of square marble, and all the front ''vermiled'' with golde.
{{right|''Ibid.'' (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''vermelet†''', ''n.'' [< OF. ''vermeillet'', somewhat red, dim. of ''vermeil'', red: see ''vermeil.''] Vermilion.
{{smaller block|<poem>O bright Regina, who made the so faire?
Who made thy colour ''vermelet'' and white?</poem>
{{right|''Court of Love'', l. 142.}}}}

'''vermeologist''' (vėr-mẹ̄-ol′ọ̄-jist), ''n.'' [< ''vermeolog-y'' + ''-ist.''] One who is versed in vermeology; a helminthologist.

'''vermeology''' (vėr-mẹ̄-ol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [Irreg. < L. ''vermis'', a worm (> NL. ''Vermes'', the worms), + Gr. ''-λογία'', < λέγειν, speak: see ''-ology.''] The knowledge or description of worms; that branch of zoölogy which treats of the ''Vermes''; helminthology.

'''Vermes''' (vėr′mēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of L. ''vermis'', a worm, = E. ''worm.''] '''1.''' Worms: formerly including animals resembling the common earthworm, but having no exact classificatory sense, and hence no standing in zoölogy.—'''2†.''' The sixth and last division of animals in the Linnean “Systema Naturæ” (1766), defined as consisting of those animals which have tentacles, cold white blood, and an inauriculate unilocular heart, and comprising all animals which Linnæus did not dispose under the five other classes ''Mammalia'', ''Aves'', ''Amphibia'', ''Pisces'', and ''Insecta'' (or vertebrates and insects). {{smaller|This class ''Vermes'' was divided into five orders, ''Intestina'', ''Mollusca'', ''Testacea'', ''Lithophyta'', and ''Zoöphyta'', comprising all invertebrates except insects, and was thus the waste-basket of Linnæus (as ''Radiata'' was of Cuvier).}}

'''3.''' One of the eight primary divisions of the animal kingdom; a subkingdom or phylum, one of the leading types of animal life, comprising all those animals which have a body-cavity (''Metazoa''), no backbone (''Invertebrata''), normally an intestinal canal (which ''Cœlentera'' have not), not a radiate structure (which ''Echinodermata'' have), legs if any not jointed (they are always jointed in ''Arthropoda''), and body vermiform if there are no legs. {{smaller|In this acceptation ''Vermes'' form a most comprehensive group, of great diversity of form, but agreeing in certain fundamental structural characters, being generally soft vermiform animals, oftenest segmented and bilaterally symmetrical, without limbs or with unjointed limbs. ''Vermes'' thus defined are approximately equivalent—(''a'') in Lamarck’s system (1801–1812), to a class of animals divided into the four orders ''Molles'', ''Rigiduli'', ''Hispiduli'', and ''Epizoariæ'' (the last including lernæan crustaceans); (''b'') in the Cuvierian classification (1817), to the whole of Cuvier’s first class of ''Articulata'' (the annelids of Lamarck, or red-blooded worms with unjointed legs) plus his second and third classes of ''Radiata'' (''Apoda'' and ''Entozoa''), plus some of his fourth class of ''Radiata'' (some ''Polypi''), plus his first order (''Rotifera'') of his fifth class of ''Radiata''; (''c'') in Huxley’s classification (1869), to the classes ''Polyzoa'', ''Scolecida'', ''Annelida'', ''Chætognatha'', and therefore to his two subkingdoms, ''Annuloida'' and ''Annulosa'', without the ''Echinodermata'' of the former, and without the ''Crustacea'', ''Arachnida'', ''Myriapoda'', and ''Insecta'' of the latter; or, in other terms, to his ''Annuloida'' minus ''Echinodermata'' and plus the whole of the anarthropodous ''Annulosa''. ''Vermes'' as here defined have been divided into seven classes: (1) ''Platyelmintha'', with three orders, respectively the turbellarian, trematoid, and cestoid worms; (2) ''Nematelmintha'', with two orders, the nematoid and acanthocephalous worms — most of these two classes, excepting the ''Turbellaria'', being entozoic or ectozoic parasites, as tapeworms, threadworms, etc.; (3) ''Chætognatha'', based on the single exceptional form ''Sagitta''; (4) ''Gephyrea'' (being Cuvier’s second order of ''Echinodermata''); (5) ''Annelida'', or ordinary segmented worms, with four orders —''Hirudinea'' (leeches), ''Oligochæta'' (earthworms, etc.), ''Polychæta'' (lobworms, sea-mice, etc.), and ''Cephalobranchia'' (tubicolous worms, etc.); (6) ''Rotifera'', the wheel-animalcules; (7) ''Polyzoa'' (by most naturalists now dissociated from ''Vermes''). The tendency at present is to break up the unmanageable group and discard the name.}}
{{smaller block|The total abandoning of the indefinite and indefensible group of ''Vermes''.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 812.}}}}
'''4.''' [''l. c.''] Plural of ''vermis''.

'''Vermetacea''' (vėr-mē-tā′sē-ä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vermetus'' + ''-acea''.] Same as ''Vermetidæ''.

'''Vermetidæ''' (vėr-met′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Vermetus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of tænioglossate gastropods, whose typical genus is ''Vermetus''; the worm-shells. {{smaller|The animal has a reduced foot, a single elongated gill, short tentacles, and the eyes at the external sides of the tentacles. The operculum is corneous and circular. The young shells are regularly conic and spiral, like those of ''Turritella''; but as they grow the whorls separate, and often become crooked or contorted.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
